title: Bawa and the Night the Lights Went Out

pages.text: Suddenly, the lights went out. The room was dark. Bawa jumped. “I cannot see anything,” he said. “Stay where you are,” said his sister Napari. “It is only a power cut.”
sentences: Suddenly, the lights went out.
The room was dark.
Bawa jumped.
“I cannot see anything,” he said.
“Stay where you are,” said his sister Napari.
“It is only a power cut.”
pages.alt: In a cosy Ghanaian living room dimly lit only by soft blue moonlight through the window, young Bawa sits close beside his calm older sister Napari.

pages.text: Napari switched on a small torch. A circle of light fell on the floor. “A torch gives light,” she said. “So does a light bulb when the power is on, and so does the sun in the day.”
sentences: Napari switched on a small torch.
A circle of light fell on the floor.
“A torch gives light,” she said.
“So does a light bulb when the power is on, and so does the sun in the day.”
pages.alt: Napari switches on a small hand torch, casting a warm golden circle of light onto the woven floor mat beside Bawa.

pages.text: “Why can I see my toy now?” asked Bawa. “Light from the torch hits your toy and bounces to your eyes,” said Napari. “We see things when light comes from them or bounces off them.”
sentences: “Why can I see my toy now?” asked Bawa.
“Light from the torch hits your toy and bounces to your eyes,” said Napari.
“We see things when light comes from them or bounces off them.”
pages.alt: Bawa smiles with curiosity as the warm beam from Napari’s torch shines directly onto his small wooden toy car on the floor.

pages.text: Their mother said, “In a power cut, stay calm and stay together. Use a torch, not a flame, and never play with matches or candles. If you see a wire on the ground, do not touch it. Tell a grown-up.”
sentences: Their mother said, “In a power cut, stay calm and stay together.
Use a torch, not a flame, and never play with matches or candles.
If you see a wire on the ground, do not touch it.
Tell a grown-up.”
pages.alt: Sitting together on the sofa in the gentle glow of the torch, their mother speaks calmly and reassuringly to Bawa and Napari.

pages.text: Bawa breathed slowly. “The dark is just the place where there is no light,” he said. They sang a quiet song and told riddles until the fear went away.
sentences: Bawa breathed slowly.
“The dark is just the place where there is no light,” he said.
They sang a quiet song and told riddles until the fear went away.
pages.alt: Cuddled happily together on the sofa in warm torchlight, Bawa, Napari and their mother clap softly and sing with relaxed smiles.

pages.text: After a while, the lights came back. “Hooray!” said Bawa. The next day, he and Napari drew bright pictures of things that give light and ways to stay safe in the dark. Bawa smiled. “Now I am not afraid.”
sentences: After a while, the lights came back.
“Hooray!” said Bawa.
The next day, he and Napari drew bright pictures of things that give light and ways to stay safe in the dark.
Bawa smiled.
“Now I am not afraid.”
pages.alt: In bright morning sunlight at a wooden table, Bawa and Napari colour cheerful wordless drawings of a shining sun, a glowing bulb and a hand torch.

activities.prompt: How do you think Bawa felt when the lights went out?

glossary.definition: A small light you hold in your hand.
What lets us see. It comes from the sun, a bulb and a torch.
Electricity that makes lights and machines work.
